design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of published studies of ketamine-associated uropathy (KAU) (Hong Kong Med J 2022;28(6):466–474, online 5 December 2022; read as the publisher's HTML full text). Embase, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched to 26 June 2020 (human studies in English, conference abstracts excluded; reference lists searched). Case series, case-cohort studies, non-randomised studies and randomised trials were eligible. 45 articles entered the qualitative synthesis and 37 the quantitative synthesis; the Results count 4890 patients (the abstract 4921). Pooled single-group prevalences of symptoms and urinary-tract findings (Table 1; random effects with double arcsine transformation, OpenMeta[Analyst]) and pooled mean questionnaire scores and urodynamic values (Table 2); cystoscopy, biopsy and treatment results are summarized narratively, treatments partly in Table 3. No comparison group enters any pool, and the included studies are neither listed nor appraised in the article. Tables 1–3 and the PRISMA flow diagram are images in the HTML; the four online appendices (PDF) were not read.
can_establish: Which symptoms, urodynamic values and imaging findings published clinical series have reported in patients with urinary problems attributed to ketamine (mostly from Hong Kong and Taiwan, up to June 2020), their average and spread across series, and which treatments those series describe.
cannot_establish: How often people who use ketamine develop urinary harm (the pooled prevalences describe patients already identified with uropathy, largely in urology services); whether the amount, frequency or duration of use, or other drugs, change the risk (not synthesized); whether any treatment, or stopping ketamine, works better than another course (no comparative or controlled evidence is pooled); or how trustworthy the pooled figures are (no risk-of-bias assessment, no heterogeneity statistics in the article, no assessment of publication bias).

sample.recruitment: Database search (Embase, MEDLINE, CENTRAL) to 26 June 2020; human studies in English; conference abstracts excluded; reference lists of included articles searched, adding none (Methods › Literature search; Results, 1st paragraph). The patients in the primary studies were mostly people presenting to urology services with urinary symptoms and a history of ketamine use; the review says most studies came from Asian countries or regions such as Taiwan and Hong Kong (Discussion › Limitations) but gives no count by country or setting.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case series, case-cohort studies, non-randomised studies and randomised controlled trials 'related to ketamine abuse and uropathy'. Excluded: editorials, commentaries, reviews, case reports, non-human studies, articles without an English full text or without any full text, and studies of ketamine used for anaesthesia (Methods › Screening process and selection criteria). There is no case definition of ketamine-associated uropathy and no criterion for how ketamine use was established.
sample.demographics: 4890 patients, 3518 men and 1372 women (72% men, editors' arithmetic); mean age 25.46 years (SD 6.03); mean duration of ketamine use 54.99 months (SD 43.54) (Results › Demographics). How these means were combined, and from how many studies, is not stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; follow-up within the primary studies is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases, English only, conference abstracts excluded, no grey literature or trial registries; one non-English article was excluded at full text (PRISMA figure). The primary studies are clinical series of patients identified because they had urinary problems, so every pooled 'prevalence' is conditional on that selection. Patient overlap between studies was checked for the pooled analyses only (Methods › Data analysis and statistical analysis). Review authors are authors of some included series (references 7 and 17, both in Table 3).

exposure.measurement: Not extracted: the review does not report how each primary study established ketamine use (self-report, urine testing or records). 'Cumulative exposure' is summarized only as a mean duration of use (54.99 months).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized: no amounts, frequency or route are reported. The Discussion cites a UK survey (Winstock et al., 2012) for an association of dose and frequency of use with the extent of urinary symptoms, and a Taiwanese series (Tsai et al., 2009) for symptoms beginning about a month after use began and worsening after a year; both are second-hand.
exposure.polysubstance: Not extracted or reported: the review does not say whether patients used other drugs, nor whether the included studies excluded or recorded them.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not systematically extracted. The review reports that abstinence was regarded as key in 11 of 19 treatment articles, that one treatment protocol required at least 6 months' abstinence before bladder reconstruction (Table 3, indications), and that surgery was effective only when patients avoided further ketamine use (four articles).

comparison.controls: None in any pooled estimate: all are single-group prevalences or means. One included study compared 13 patients with ketamine cystitis with 16 with interstitial cystitis (Discussion › Clinical diagnosis, 1st paragraph), and one compared voided volume by length of abstinence in 66 people (Mak et al.; Discussion › Management); neither is pooled.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not extracted: urinary history before ketamine use, other bladder disease, infection and other causes of symptoms are not reported, although the Discussion recommends excluding infection and stones in practice.

outcomes.instruments: Symptoms as reported by each study (frequency, urgency, suprapubic or bladder pain, nocturia, dysuria, haematuria, incontinence); upper-tract findings on imaging (hydronephrosis, vesicoureteral reflux, ureteral stricture) and impaired renal function; questionnaires: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), Interstitial Cystitis Symptom Index and Problem Index (ICSI, ICPI), Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency score (PUF), visual analogue scale (VAS); urodynamics: functional bladder capacity, cystometric and maximum cystometric capacity, voided volume, maximum flow rate (Qmax), detrusor overactivity; cystoscopy and biopsy findings (narrative); treatment responses as each study defined them.
outcomes.validity_norms: The questionnaires were developed for prostate symptoms (IPSS) and interstitial cystitis (ICSI, ICPI, PUF); the review cites one validation of a Chinese PUF version in people who used street ketamine (Ng et al., 2012, proposing a threshold of 17) and interstitial-cystitis thresholds for ICSI (7 of 15) and ICPI (5 of 14) (Discussion › Clinical diagnosis, 2nd paragraph). No reference values for bladder capacity or flow are given.
outcomes.operationalization: No case definition of ketamine-associated uropathy is stated (the Discussion notes there are no standard diagnostic criteria). A symptom counts as present as each study reported it; 'improvement' after treatment is each study's own definition (reduced treatment, symptom relief, capacity, 'responded').
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: 22 pooled descriptive estimates (12 prevalences in Table 1, 10 means in Table 2) and no hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Records were screened by at least two independent reviewers with a third senior reviewer for disagreements; data were extracted on a standardised form, with no statement that extraction was duplicated or checked.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled estimates with 95% CIs. Prevalences (Table 1; 37 studies, 4314 patients): frequency 77.1% (56.9 to 92.2); urgency 69.9% (48.8 to 87.3); detrusor overactivity 63.9% (45.6 to 80.3); suprapubic pain 60.4% (35.3 to 82.9); nocturia 58.0% (38.5 to 76.2); dysuria 49.8% (28.5 to 71.1); haematuria 46.3% (22.6 to 71.0); incontinence 43.9% (21.0 to 68.2); hydronephrosis 30.2% (22.0 to 39.2); vesicoureteral reflux 22.0% (12.4 to 33.5); ureteral stricture 19.4% (7.3 to 35.5); impaired renal function 8.3% (4.8 to 12.6). Means (Table 2): IPSS 11.61 (6.37 to 16.84), n=1366, 5 studies; ICSI 11.11 (4.12 to 18.09) and ICPI 10.24 (3.84 to 16.64), n=1263, 5 studies; PUF 21.66 (20.12 to 23.20), n=750; VAS 6.46 (4.62 to 8.30), n=161; functional bladder capacity 95.23 mL (63.57 to 126.88), n=717; cystometric capacity 97.37 mL (58.23 to 136.51), n=491; maximum cystometric capacity 202.09 mL (169.06 to 235.13), n=140; voided volume 113.31 mL (59.44 to 167.19), n=630; Qmax 8.69 mL/s (5.54 to 11.83), n=451. No I², tau² or prediction interval is reported for any estimate, and the number of studies is not given for most.
analysis.covariates: None: no subgroup, sensitivity or meta-regression analysis (for example by country, setting, design or duration of use) is reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review states it followed the PRISMA statement (2009 version cited).
analysis.selective_reporting: Heterogeneity statistics (planned as Cochran's Q and I²), forest plots and, for most estimates, the number of studies behind each pooled figure are not in the article; the text refers to online Appendices 2–4, which were not read. Treatment results are a selection of studies in Table 3 with no stated rule for inclusion, and the text cites studies absent from the table's results (Lee et al., Meng et al., Zeng et al., Sihra et al.).
analysis.power: Not applicable. Intervals are wide for most symptoms (frequency 56.9% to 92.2%; suprapubic pain 35.3% to 82.9%), consistent with large differences between studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among patients in published series of ketamine-associated uropathy (37 studies, 4314 patients, retrospective by the authors' account and mostly from Hong Kong and Taiwan), frequency (77.1%), urgency (69.9%), suprapubic pain (60.4%) and nocturia (58.0%) were the symptoms reported most often, with wide intervals; hydronephrosis was reported in 30.2% and impaired renal function in 8.3%. Pooled functional bladder capacity was 95 mL and maximum flow 8.7 mL/s. Treatment results are a narrative account of uncontrolled series, and abstinence was regarded as key in 11 of 19 treatment articles.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that ketamine abstinence “was necessary for improvement”; the conclusion calls abstinence essential and a tiered approach preferred, and the Discussion says abstinence is consistently effective regardless of severity (Discussion › Management, 1st paragraph). No analysis in the review compares patients who stopped with patients who continued: the support is a count of articles that regarded abstinence as key, one comparison of voided volume by length of abstinence (Mak et al.), reports of hydronephrosis resolving in patients who stopped, and surgical series in which abstinence was a condition of treatment, none with a control group and none appraised for risk of bias. The abstract and conclusion also present the pooled figures as the clinical picture of KAU without saying that they come from patients selected because they had urinary problems, so they cannot be read as how often people who use ketamine develop these problems. The abstract's patient count (4921) differs from the Results (4890).

timeline.event: Shahani et al.: 9 patients in Toronto, proposing ketamine-associated ulcerative cystitis as a new entity; cited by this review as the first description and included among its treatment studies.

Chu et al. (BJU Int): 59 patients from two Hong Kong urology units, described by this review as showing upper-tract involvement (hydronephrosis, papillary necrosis, raised creatinine). Not read for this card (publisher full text not accessible in this round).
Winstock et al.: online survey of 3806 respondents, cited by this review for a relation of dose and frequency of ketamine use to urinary symptoms.
This review: 45 articles, 4890 patients, search to June 2020.

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive synthesis of clinical series; its authors call for prospective studies and standardized workup. It does not answer how common urinary harm is among people who use ketamine, which needs community samples such as the survey of Winstock et al. (2012); studies published after June 2020 are not covered.

funding.funder: No specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (Funding/support statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: MCS Wong, CF Ng and JYC Teoh are editors of the journal and were not involved in the peer review of this article; the other authors disclosed no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Surgery (urology), The Chinese University of Hong Kong; University College London; Royal Derby Hospital; University of Leeds; The Jockey Club School of Public Health and Primary Care, CUHK. Review authors CH Yee and CF Ng are authors of included series (references 7 and 17, both in Table 3), and Yee and Teoh of reference 24, cited in the Discussion; no procedure for handling the authors' own studies is described (no study was appraised). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use ketamine recruited outside urology services, with verified ketamine and other drug use, repeated standardized measurement of urinary symptoms (a validated questionnaire), bladder capacity and upper-tract imaging, and follow-up of those who stop and those who continue; and controlled comparisons of the treatments offered, analysed by whether patients stopped using ketamine.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The aim (to summarise manifestations, assessments and management of KAU) names a population and outcomes in general terms, but the inclusion criteria give only designs and a topic: no case definition of the population, no criterion for how ketamine use was established, and, for the treatment question, no interventions, comparators or outcome measures.
No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review cites PRISMA only.
Case series, case-cohort and non-randomised studies and trials were eligible, and reviews and case reports excluded, without an explanation for the choice.

Three databases with keywords and MeSH terms (strategy in online Appendix 1, not read) and reference lists, but English only and conference abstracts excluded without a stated reason, and no grey literature, trial registries or contact with experts; the search ended about two and a half years before publication. Unjustified limits on language or publication type give 'no' under AMSTAR 2 as written (project decision p-amstar2-item4).
All records were screened independently by at least two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third senior reviewer (Methods › Screening process and selection criteria).
Extraction on a standardised form; no statement that two reviewers extracted or checked the data (Methods › Data extraction).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The PRISMA figure gives counts of full-text exclusions by reason (110 wrong study type, 23 unrelated to urology, 4 animal studies, 1 non-English) but no list of the excluded studies; the online appendices, as the text describes them, hold the search strategy and per-outcome results.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The article neither lists the 45 included studies nor describes their populations, settings, designs, sample sizes or how uropathy and ketamine use were established; only pooled demographics are given, and the reader cannot tell which of the studies cited in the text were among the 45.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the included studies is described or reported.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling with double arcsine transformation suits proportions, and patient overlap was checked; but combining was justified only by a rule (more than two studies with over 100 patients) across series with different case definitions, settings and workups, and although heterogeneity was to be measured with Q and I², no value is reported in the article for any estimate (they may be in the unread appendices), nor, for most estimates, the number of studies.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment was done, so its impact on the pooled estimates was not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations note that all studies were retrospective and heterogeneous, but the conclusions (abstinence essential, tiered treatment preferred) are drawn without considering the biases of uncontrolled series.
The limitations attribute heterogeneity to variations in workup and treatment, but it is neither quantified in the article nor investigated (no subgroup or sensitivity analysis).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No specific funding; three authors are journal editors and were not involved in the peer review; the others declare no conflicts. That review authors wrote included series is not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Seven critical items fail (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15), so confidence in the results is critically low under AMSTAR 2. This judges how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as summaries: the review is a useful catalogue of what clinical series of KAU have reported, and its pooled symptom prevalences and urodynamic values may be cited as describing patients in those series (mostly from Hong Kong and Taiwan, to June 2020), with their wide intervals. It may not be cited for how often people who use ketamine develop urinary problems, for the effectiveness of any treatment, or for abstinence being necessary for improvement. The appendices (PDF) were not read; they may hold heterogeneity statistics and per-study data, which could change items 11 and 14 but not the overall rating.

key_findings.finding: Search: Embase, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials to 26 June 2020, with keywords and MeSH terms for ketamine use, urinary tracts and urological examinations; human studies in English only, conference abstracts excluded; reference lists searched, adding no articles; search strategy in online Appendix 1.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Literature search; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Selection and extraction: screening by at least two independent reviewers with a third senior reviewer for disagreements; eligible designs case series, case-cohort studies, non-randomised studies and randomised trials; excluded editorials, commentaries, reviews, case reports, non-human studies, non-English or unavailable full texts and anaesthetic use. Extraction on a standardised form covered age, sex, cumulative ketamine exposure, symptoms, urinalysis and renal function, urodynamics, imaging, cystoscopy and biopsy, questionnaire scores, and treatments with their responses.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Screening process and selection criteria; Methods › Data extraction

key_findings.finding: Flow: 1365 records from database searches; 913 after removal of duplicates; 730 excluded on screening; 183 full texts, of which 138 were excluded (110 wrong study type, 23 unrelated to urology, 4 animal studies, 1 non-English article); 45 articles in the qualitative synthesis and 37 studies in the quantitative synthesis.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure (PRISMA flow diagram)
key_findings.note: The flow diagram is an image; its numbers were read from it and agree with the text (913 − 730 − 138 = 45, editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Pooling: OpenMeta[Analyst], used when results were available from more than two studies with more than 100 patients; random-effects models with double arcsine transformation; heterogeneity to be tested with Cochran's Q (P<0.10) and measured with I² (over 50% taken as significant); studies in each pool reviewed to exclude patient overlap.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data analysis and statistical analysis

key_findings.finding: Patients: 4890 (3518 men, 1372 women), mean age 25.46 years (SD 6.03), mean duration of ketamine use 54.99 months (SD 43.54).
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics; Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 4921 patients in 45 articles; the Results give 4890 (3518 + 1372 = 4890).

key_findings.finding: Lower urinary tract symptoms, pooled prevalence among patients with KAU (37 studies, 4314 patients): frequency 77.1% (95% CI 56.9 to 92.2), urgency 69.9% (48.8 to 87.3), suprapubic pain 60.4% (35.3 to 82.9), nocturia 58.0% (38.5 to 76.2), dysuria 49.8% (28.5 to 71.1), haematuria 46.3% (22.6 to 71.0), incontinence 43.9% (21.0 to 68.2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical manifestations, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Table 1 is an image, transcribed from the rendered page; it gives no number of studies, patients or I² per symptom (online Appendix 2, not read). These are proportions of patients identified with uropathy, not of people who use ketamine.

key_findings.finding: Upper urinary tract and urodynamic findings, pooled prevalence: hydronephrosis 30.2% (22.0 to 39.2), vesicoureteral reflux 22.0% (12.4 to 33.5), ureteral stricture 19.4% (7.3 to 35.5), impaired renal function 8.3% (4.8 to 12.6), detrusor overactivity 63.9% (45.6 to 80.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical manifestations, 1st paragraph; Results › Bladder assessments, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The text rounds ureteral stricture to about 20% and impaired renal function to about 10%; the table gives 19.4% and 8.3%.

key_findings.finding: Symptom scores, pooled means (13 studies, 2135 patients): IPSS 11.61 (6.37 to 16.84), 5 studies, n=1366; ICSI 11.11 (4.12 to 18.09) and ICPI 10.24 (3.84 to 16.64), 5 studies, n=1263; PUF 21.66 (20.12 to 23.20), n=750; VAS 6.46 (4.62 to 8.30), n=161. The Discussion sets these beside thresholds from other studies: ICSI 7 and ICPI 5 for interstitial cystitis, and PUF 17 for serious urological consequences in people who used street ketamine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom scores; Table 2; Discussion › Clinical diagnosis, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 2 is an image, transcribed from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Bladder measures, pooled means (15 studies, 1221 patients with capacity data): functional bladder capacity 95.23 mL (63.57 to 126.88), n=717; cystometric capacity 97.37 mL (58.23 to 136.51), n=491; maximum cystometric capacity 202.09 mL (169.06 to 235.13), n=140; voided volume 113.31 mL (59.44 to 167.19), n=630; maximum flow rate 8.69 mL/s (5.54 to 11.83), n=451.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bladder assessments, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Cystoscopy and biopsy (14 studies, narrative only): epithelial inflammation, erythematous patches, neovascularisation and ulceration, with petechial haemorrhage in severe disease; urothelial denudation and focal reactive changes, and in the lamina propria granulation tissue, vascular congestion, oedema and infiltrating lymphocytes, eosinophils and mast cells; perivesical fibrosis in some patients. No pooled frequencies; the review cites Chu et al.'s 71% with inflammatory changes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bladder assessments, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Treatment (19 articles): approaches varied with no consistent pattern; abstinence was regarded as key in 11 of the 19. Oral treatment (Table 3): Yee et al., n=290 (anti-inflammatory and non-opioid analgesics, anticholinergics), 234 (80.7%) improved on EuroQol VAS, PUF score and functional bladder capacity; Yee et al., n=62 (opioid analgesics, pregabalin), 42 (67.7%) improved; Wu et al., n=24, improvements in voided volume, micturition interval, night-time voiding and PUF score; Shahani et al. (9 patients) reported relief with pentosan polysulphate combined with abstinence, and Tsai et al. 11 patients with poor responses to anti-inflammatory drugs, anticholinergics and antibiotics.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatments; Results › Treatments › Oral treatment; Table 3
key_findings.note: Table 3 is an image, transcribed from the rendered page. Uncontrolled series; 'improved' is each study's own definition.

key_findings.finding: Intravesical hyaluronan (7 studies): the text says 30 of 34 patients in six studies improved and the seventh study (2 patients) showed no improvement; Table 3 lists Yee et al. 5 of 8 able to reduce treatment, Chen et al. 2 of 2 with less suprapubic pain, Lai et al. 4 of 6 with better bladder capacity, Li et al. 5 of 7 responding, and Tsai et al. (n=6) improved symptoms without a count.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatments › Intravesical treatment; Table 3
key_findings.note: The text's 30 of 34 cannot be reconciled with Table 3 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Hydrodistension: Wu et al. 35 of 47 (74.5%) improved in voided volume, PUF score, frequency and nocturia; Chang et al. 14 of 20 (70.0%) and Li et al. 10 of 14 (71.4%) had symptomatic relief. With botulinum toxin A injection, Zeng et al. reported general improvement and Sihra et al. subjective relief in 4 of 29.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatments › Surgical treatment, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Bladder reconstruction (augmentation cystoplasty, or cystectomy with neobladder or ileal conduit; 5 studies, all reporting efficacy in advanced ketamine cystitis): Lee et al. 26 of 26 improved in capacity, voided volume and residual volume; Hung et al. 8 of 8 improved in capacity, renal function and pain. Table 3: Jhang et al. (n=28) cystometric capacity 52.7 ± 29.7 to 327 ± 69.4 mL, Qmax 6.94 ± 4.32 to 13.7 ± 4.96 mL/s, voided volume 44.1 ± 28.3 to 250.7 ± 133.4 mL, post-void residual 8.08 ± 19.2 to 82.6 ± 91.5 mL; Hung et al. (n=8) functional capacity 47.75 ± 10.07 to 273.13 ± 54.96 mL, VAS 6.0 ± 1.2 to 1.75 ± 0.89; Ng et al. (n=4) maximal capacity 37.5 to 400–500 mL. Indications listed include intractable symptoms after conservative treatment, persistently low capacity, cystometric capacity under 100 mL and, in one protocol, at least 6 months' abstinence; surgery was effective only when patients avoided further ketamine use (four studies).
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatments › Surgical treatment, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: Before–after values in uncontrolled surgical series. Table 3 labels the rise in post-void residual as an improvement (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Abstinence: the Discussion states that abstinence is consistently effective regardless of severity, citing Mak et al. (66 people: maximal voided volume 387 mL after at least a year of abstinence against 243 mL after less than 3 months) and Yee et al. (hydronephrosis resolving spontaneously in patients who stopped).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Management of ketamine-associated uropathy, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: As the review describes it, Mak et al. compared people with different lengths of abstinence (a contrast between groups), not the same people before and after stopping; neither comparison is pooled or appraised.

key_findings.finding: Dose and duration: the Discussion says symptom severity may be associated with chronicity and dose, citing a UK survey of 3806 people (Winstock et al., 2012) in which dose and frequency of use were associated with the extent of urinary symptoms, and a Taiwanese series (Tsai et al.) in which symptoms began about 1 month after use began and were considerably worse after 1 year.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Clinical presentation of ketamine-associated uropathy, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand; cite the primary studies (winstock_2012 has its own card).

key_findings.finding: Mechanism: unknown. Hypotheses cited: direct toxic damage, microvascular injury, an autoimmune reaction in the urothelium and submucosa, or (less likely) unrecognised bacteriuria (Chu et al.); a dysfunctional urothelium with a defective glycosaminoglycan layer (Wu et al.); and hypersensitivity, supported by higher serum immunoglobulin E in patients with KAU than in controls (Jhang et al.).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Potential pathophysiology of ketamine-associated uropathy, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Diagnosis: ketamine cystitis resembles interstitial cystitis clinically and histologically; onset at age 30 or younger is described as a clue, since interstitial cystitis usually begins at 40 or older. In one study (13 patients with ketamine cystitis, 16 with interstitial cystitis), ketamine cystitis showed more severe bladder dysfunction, smaller capacity, thicker bladder wall and greater subjective discomfort (a lower VAS score, as the review puts it). The review recommends questionnaires, urinalysis, culture and imaging first, with cystoscopy only later if indicated, because routine cystoscopy may discourage young patients from further care.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Clinical diagnosis of ketamine-associated uropathy, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: all included studies were retrospective; studies were heterogeneous because of variations in workup and treatment; treatment efficacy could not be fully assessed because baseline characteristics were inconsistently described; most studies came from Asian countries or regions such as Taiwan and Hong Kong.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations

key_findings.finding: Background (Hong Kong Central Registry of Drug Abuse, 69th report): ketamine was the most commonly reported psychotropic substance in 2009–2014, with 5280 people reported for it in 2009; 405 were reported in 2019, 7.3% of all people reported for drug use that year.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand; cite the registry report itself (report R10 on the ketamine list).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 4921 patients in the 45 included articles; the Results give 4890 (3518 men and 1372 women).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Demographics
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 4890 from the Results; the abstract's count is not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: The intravesical-treatment paragraph says 30 of 34 patients in six studies improved, but Table 3's results for five of those studies are 5 of 8 (Yee et al.), 2 of 2 (Chen et al.), 4 of 6 (Lai et al.), 5 of 7 (Li et al.) and an unquantified improvement in Tsai et al. (n=6); the sixth study (Meng et al.) is not in the table. With the table's counts, at most 27 could have improved: 16 counted in four studies, plus all 6 in Tsai et al. and all 5 in Meng et al., whose size is implied by 34 minus the table's 29 (editors' arithmetic), unless the text counts improvements the table does not. The outcomes also differ between studies (reduced treatment, pain, capacity, 'responded').
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Treatments › Intravesical treatment; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The 30 of 34 should not be cited; the per-study results in Table 3 are the usable figures, each with its own outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 'improved post-void residual' after bladder reconstruction in Jhang et al. (n=28) with values that rose from 8.08 ± 19.2 to 82.6 ± 91.5 mL, and the text counts residual volume among the improvements in Lee et al.; the review does not explain in what sense a larger residual is an improvement.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3 (bladder reconstruction, Jhang et al.); Results › Treatments › Surgical treatment, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The residual-volume result should not be cited as a benefit of reconstruction without the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 and the oral-treatment paragraph attribute results for oral treatment (n=24) and bladder reconstruction (n=10) to reference 18, which the reference list gives as a study of bladder wall thickness in bladder pain syndrome and the Discussion describes as a comparison of 13 patients with ketamine cystitis and 16 with interstitial cystitis; the staging study with tiered medication, hydrodistension and reconstruction is reference 8 (Wu et al., World J Urol 2016), cited for the hydrodistension row.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 3; Results › Treatments › Oral treatment; Discussion › Clinical diagnosis, 1st paragraph; references 8 and 18
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a citation-numbering error (not checked against the primary papers); the source of these two rows must be confirmed before they are cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations state that all included studies were retrospective, but one included study, cited for the largest oral-treatment and intravesical results in Table 3, is titled as a prospective case series (reference 7, Yee et al., Urology 2015).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Discussion › Limitations; Table 3; reference 7
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but it shows the design of the included studies was not tabulated or checked; the review gives no count of designs.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods plan Cochran's Q and I² for heterogeneity, but no Q, I², tau² or prediction interval is reported for any pooled estimate in the article, and Tables 1 and 2 give no number of studies for most estimates (they refer to online Appendices 2–4, which were not read).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Methods › Data analysis and statistical analysis; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The spread between studies cannot be judged from the article; the wide confidence intervals are the only sign of it, and single pooled prevalences describe no particular clinical population.

reporting_issues.issue: The surgical results come from two series from the same group (Lee et al., 26 of 26 improved, in the text; Jhang et al., n=28, in Table 3; both with Jhang and Kuo as authors), and the review does not say whether their patients overlap; overlap was checked only for the pooled analyses.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Treatments › Surgical treatment, 2nd paragraph; Table 3; references 10 and 11
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts of patients improving after reconstruction should not be summed across these series.
